---
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
(Fermat's Little Theorem)
Let $p$ be a prime number, $a\in\mathbb{Z}_p$, and $a\neq 0$; then $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}.$
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{euler} (Euler’s Theorem)
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $a\in \mathbb{Z}_n$ such that $\gcd(a,n)=1$, then $a^{\varphi (n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, where $\varphi (n)$ is Euler’s $\varphi$-function.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$; we say that $a$ is an idempotent element of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ if $a^2 \equiv a \pmod{n}$. Thus, $0$ and $1$ are always idempotent elements for every ring $\mathbb{Z}_n.$ These two idempotents are always present and are considered trivial.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $a\in \mathbb{Z}_n$, then $a^{\varphi (n)} \equiv b \pmod{n}$, where $b$ is an idempotent element of $\mathbb{Z}_n.$
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $n=p_1^{r_1}\ldots p_k^{r_k}$ be the factorial decomposition of $n.$ We will consider two cases, depending on whether each $p_i$ divides $a$ or not. If we first assume that $p_i\mid a,$ then, since $$r_i=1+(r_i-1)\ \leq 2^{r_i-1}\leq p_i^{r_i-1}\leq p_i^{r_i-1}(p_i-1)\leq\varphi (n),$$ we have that $a^{\varphi (n)} \equiv 0 \pmod{p_i^{r_i}}$. On the other hand, if $p_i\nmid a,$ then by Euler’s Theorem (\ref{euler}) and the fact that $\varphi \left(p_i^{r_i}\right)\mid\varphi (n),$ we obtain $a^{\varphi (n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i^{r_i}}$. Therefore, in both cases $a^{\varphi (n)}(a^{\varphi (n)}-1) \equiv 0 \pmod{p_i^{r_i}},$ and thus $b$ is idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n = p_1^{r_1} \ldots p_k^{r_k}$; then $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has exactly $2^k$ idempotent elements, including the trivial elements $0$ and $1$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The proof is straightforward and can be seen in detail in \cite{vass2016composite}; it uses the fact that every congruence equation of the form $a^2 \equiv a \pmod{p_i^{r_i}}$ has only two solutions, $0$ and $1$, therefore each idempotent of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is uniquely associated, via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, with a sequence $(a_1,\ldots ,a_k)$ where $a_i\in \{0,1\}$. Thus, counting all possibilities, the total is $2^k.$
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
The number of idempotents in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is equal to $2^{\omega (n)},$ where $\omega(n)$ is the function that returns the number of prime divisors of $n$ (one if $n$ is a prime number). Therefore, the only idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}_p,$ where $p$ is prime, are $0$ and $1$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $a$ and $b$ be idempotents in $\mathbb{Z}_n$; then $a$ and $b$ are said to be orthogonal if $ab \equiv 0 \pmod n$.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{orta1-a}
Given an idempotent $a\in \mathbb{Z}_n$, we have that $1-a$ is also an idempotent and that $a$ and $1-a$ are orthogonal. In particular, all idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are zero divisors in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ and therefore lack a multiplicative inverse in this same ring.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Orthogonality is evident simply by doing the math, since $a(1-a) \equiv a^2 - a \equiv a - a \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$. It remains to be shown that $1-a$ is indeed an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$, but this is also straightforward since $(1-a)^2 \equiv 1+a^2-2a \equiv 1+a-2a \equiv 1-a \pmod{n}.$
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{ilc}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be a square-free number, the following holds:

\begin{enumerate}
\item The idempotent elements of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are exactly those of the form $d^{\varphi (n)},$ where $d\mid n.$
\item The equation $$x^{\varphi (n)}\equiv \left(\frac{n}{d_0}\right)^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n}$$ has exactly $\varphi (d_0)$ solutions in $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
\item $\sum_{a\in \mathbb{Z}_n}{a^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi (d)\cdot \left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}}\pmod{n}.$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We know that if $n = p_1 \ldots p_k$, then $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has $2^k$ idempotents. We know that every element $a$ of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ that satisfies $a^{\varphi (n)}$ is idempotent; therefore, in particular, $\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}$ is idempotent, which is equivalent to saying that $d^{\varphi (n)}$ is idempotent. Furthermore, there are $2^k$ idempotents of this form, since they correspond to different ways of grouping divisors of $n$, which in total are $$\binom{n}{0}+\binom{n}{1}+\ldots \binom{n}{k}=2^k.$$ It suffices, therefore, to show that all these idempotents are distinct from one another.

Suppose that two of them are congruent, that is, $$d^{\varphi (n)}\equiv e^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n},$$ with $d,e\mid n.$ Since $d \neq e,$ there exists, without loss of generality, at least one prime divisor $q$ of $d$ such that $q$ does not divide $e. $ Then $d\equiv 0 \pmod{q}$ and therefore $d^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 0 \pmod{q}.$ On the other hand, $\gcd(q,e)=1$ and by \ref{euler}, $e^{\varphi(q)} \equiv 1 \pmod{q}.$ Since $q \mid n$, we have that $\varphi(q) \mid \varphi(n)$ and $e^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{q}. $ But we assumed that $d^{\varphi (n)}\equiv e^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n},$ and therefore $d^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 1 \pmod{q},$ which is impossible. Therefore, $d^{\varphi (n)}\not\equiv e^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n}.$

For the second part, we consider the equation $$x^{\varphi (n)}\equiv \left(\frac{n}{d_0}\right)^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n}.$$ Suppose that $\frac{n}{d_0}=q_1\ldots q_{k_0}$ with $q_j\in\{p_1\ldots p_k\} .$ We have that $\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}$ is congruent to $0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{p_i}$ if $p_i$ is equal to some $q_j$ and to $1$ otherwise, using the same reasoning as before. In the first case, the equation $$x^{\varphi (n)}\equiv \left(\frac{n}{d_0}\right)^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{p_i}$$ has a single solution; in the second case, we have that $$x^{\varphi (n)}\equiv x^{\varphi (p_i)\ \varphi\left(\frac{n}{p_i}\right)}\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$$ using Fermat’s Little Theorem, and therefore, since $p_i$ is a prime number, there are exactly $p_i-1=\varphi (p_i)$ solutions. Applying this reasoning for each $p_i$, the equation has a number of solutions equal to $$\prod_{p_i\nmid\frac{n}{d_0}}\varphi (p_i)=\prod_{p_i\mid d_0}\varphi (p_i)=\varphi (d_0).$$

For the last part, in the previous section it was stated that every element $a$ of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ satisfies that $a^{\varphi (n)}$ is idempotent. Therefore, there exists a divisor $d$ of $n$ such that $$a^{\varphi (n)}\equiv\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n},$$ and there are $\varphi (d)$ of them in total. Since $a$ cannot generate two distinct idempotents, and $a^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ if and only if $a\equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ because $n$ is square-free, it follows that $$\sum_{a\in \mathbb{Z}_n}{a^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi (d)\cdot \left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}}\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
If we define on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ the relation $a\sim b \iff a^{\varphi (n)}\equiv b^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n},$ then this relation is trivially an equivalence relation and defines a quotient group, which we have shown to be precisely the group of idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}_n. $ Each class of this group can be represented as $\left[\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}\right],$ with $d\mid n.$ Furthermore, each class has exactly $\varphi (d)$ elements of $\mathbb{Z}_n.$
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{ab1}
Let $n=ab,$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1.$ Then $a^{\varphi (n)}+b^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 1 \pmod{n}. $ In particular, if $n$ is square-free, $d^{\varphi (n)}+\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ for every divisor $d$ of $n$.
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
On the one hand, we have that $$a^{\varphi (n)}+b^ {\varphi (n)}\equiv b^{\varphi (n)} \equiv b^{\varphi (ab)} \equiv \left(b^{\varphi (a)}\right)^{\varphi (b)} \equiv 1 \pmod{a},$$ using \ref{euler} and the fact that $a,b$ are relatively prime. Similarly, $a^{\varphi (n)}+b^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 1 \pmod{b}.$ This system has a unique solution modulo $n$ by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and therefore we must have $a^{\varphi (n)}+b^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 1 \pmod{n}.$
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
Using the same reasoning, it can be shown that if we take $n=a_1 \ldots a_k$ such that $\gcd(a_i,a_j)=1$ for all $1\leq i,j \leq k$, then $\sum_{i=1}^k{{a_i}^{\varphi(n)}}\equiv k-1 \pmod{n}.$
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{semiprimo}
If $n$ is a semiprime, then $\sum_{i=1}^n{{i}^{\varphi(n)}} \equiv \varphi (n)-1 \pmod{n}.$
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If we consider $n=pq,$ in particular it is square-free, by Theorem \ref{ilc}, $$\sum_{i=1}^n{i^{\varphi(n)}}\equiv\varphi (1)n^{\varphi (n)}+\varphi (p)q^{\varphi (n)}+\varphi (q)p^{\varphi (n)}+\varphi (n)1^{\varphi (n)}\equiv$$ $$\equiv\varphi (p)q^{\varphi (n)}+\varphi (q)p^{\varphi (n)}+\varphi (n) \equiv \varphi (n)-q^{\varphi (n)}-p^{\varphi (n)} \pmod{n}. $$ By result \ref{ab1}, $p^{\varphi (n)}+q^{\varphi (n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ and therefore we have proven it.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{ilc2}
If $n=p_1\ldots p_k$ is square-free, then $$\sum_{i=1}^n{i^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv \sum_{p_i\mid n}{-\frac{n}{p_i}}\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We know from Theorem \ref{ilc} that $$\sum_{a\in \mathbb{Z}_n}{a^{\varphi (n)}}=\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi (d)\cdot \left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}}.$$ Let’s compute this sum modulo $p_i. $ We have that if $p_i\mid\frac{n}{d}$ then $\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)} \equiv 0 \pmod{p_i},$ and if $p_i \nmid\frac{n}{d}$, then $\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i}.$ Therefore

$$\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi (d)\cdot \left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}} \equiv \sum_{\substack{d\mid n \\ p_i\nmid\frac{n}{d}}}{\varphi (d)}\equiv$$

$$\equiv \sum_{\substack{d\mid n \\ p_i\mid d}}{\varphi (d)} \equiv \sum_{d\mid \frac{n}{p_i}}{\varphi (p_i)\varphi (d)} \equiv \sum_{d\mid \frac{n}{p_i}}{-\varphi (d)} \equiv -\frac{n}{p_i} \pmod{p_i}.$$

Therefore, by the uniqueness of the Chinese Remainder Theorem, we have already obtained the desired result.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- obs-1: body_md -->
\label{c-vs}It is important to note that Corollary \ref{ilc2} is a special case of a result by Carlitz and von Staudt, which can be found in \cite{carlitz1961staudt} and states that, if $k>1$ and $n$ is even, then

$$\sum_{i=1}^n{i^k}=\sum_{\substack{p\mid n \\ p-1\mid k}}{-\frac{n}{p}\pmod{n}}.$$

In our case, since $n$ is square-free and $k=\varphi(n),$ we have that $k$ is even since $\varphi(n)$ is always even for any value of $n$ greater than or equal to $3$ (although Corollary \ref{ilc2} also holds for $n=2$). On the other hand, it is immediately clear that $p-1\mid k$ for every divisor $p$ of $n$, and we therefore satisfy the conditions of the proposition.
<!-- end obs-1 -->
<!-- obs-2: body_md -->
This last result leads to one of the most widely used characte\-rizations of Giuga numbers, which is due to Giuga himself \cite{giuga1950presumibile}, and states that $n$ is a Giuga number if and only if 

$$\sum_{p\mid n}{\frac{1}{p}}-\prod_{p\mid n}{\frac{1}{p}}\in\mathbb{N}.$$

To arrive at this, we need only consider the equality 

$$\sum_{p_i\mid n}{-\frac{n}{p_i}}\equiv -1\pmod{n},$$

since $n$ is a Giuga number if $$\sum_{i=1}^n{i^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv -1\pmod{n},$$ and the calculations follow naturally. It may seem that we need to add the additional condition that $n$ be square-free, but, as we will see in the next section, the same result can be deduced for any value of $n$.
<!-- end obs-2 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
Given $n\in\mathbb{N},$ we say that $a$ is a nilpotent of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ if there exists a positive $k$ such that $a^k\equiv 0 \pmod{n}.$
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
Given $n\in\mathbb{N},$ $n=p_1^{r_1}\ldots p_k^{r_k},$ the radical of $n$ is defined as $m=p_1\ldots p_k,$ that is, the greatest square-free divisor of $n,$ and is denoted by $m=\textup{rad} (n).$
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
The nilpotents of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are the multiples of the radical of $n$, and in fact the radical of $n$ is the smallest non-trivial nilpotent of $\mathbb{Z}_n.$
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem1}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $m=\textup{rad}(n)$. Then $m^s\varphi(n) = n\varphi(m^s)$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $n=p_1^{r_1}\ldots p_k^{r_k},$ then $$m^s\varphi (n) = \left(\prod_{i=1}^k{p_i^s}\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^k{p_i^{r_i}-p_i^ {r_i-1}}\right) =$$ $$=\left(\prod_{i=1}^k{p_i^{r_i-1}\cdot p_i}\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^k{p_i^{s-1}(p_i-1)}\right) = n\varphi (m^s).$$
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem2}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $m=\textup{rad} (n). $ Suppose that $n=p_1^{r_1}\ldots p_k^{r_k},$ and let $s\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n\nmid m^s.$ Then, if $r_i>s$, $p_i^{r_i-s}\mid \binom{\varphi (n)}{s}.$
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Suppose that $s=1,$ then $$\binom{\varphi (n)}{1}=\varphi (n)=\varphi \left (p_i^{r_i}\right)\cdot\varphi\left(\frac{n}{p_i^{r_i}}\right),$$ and $\varphi\left( p_i^{r_i}\right)=p_i^ {r_i-1}(p_i-1),$ so $p_i^{r_i-1}\mid \binom{\varphi (n)}{1}.$

In the general case, we have that

$$\binom{\varphi (n)}{s}=\frac{\varphi (n)-s+1}{s} \binom{\varphi (n)}{s-1}=\ldots =$$

$$= \frac{\left( \varphi (n)-s+1\right)\left( \varphi (n)-s+2\right)\ldots\left( \varphi (n)-1\right)}{s(s-1)\ldots\cdot 2}\cdot\binom{\varphi (n)}{1}.$$

By the base case, we know that $p_i^{r_i-1}\mid \binom{\varphi (n)}{1}$, so $p_i^{r_i-s}\mid p_i^{r_i-1}\mid \binom{\varphi (n)}{1}$. We have $p_i^{s-1}$ left over, but $p_i$ will divide $s(s-1)\ldots\cdot 2=s!$ several times. If we denote $x_s(p_i)$ as the multiplicity of $p_i$ in $s!$, a classic result of Legendre, which can be read in detail in \cite{aigner1999proofs}, tells us that

$$x_s(p_i)=\sum_{j\geq 1}{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p_i^j}\right\rfloor},$$

but since $\lfloor x \rfloor < x,$ we have that $$\frac{x_s(p_i)}{s} < \frac{1}{p_i} + \frac{1}{p_i^2} + \ldots = \frac{1}{p_i-1}. $$ The worst-case scenario is $p_i=2,$ which leads to $x_s(2)<s,$ but since we have $s-1$ times the factor $p_i$ left over (twice in this case), we can cancel out all occurrences of $p_i$ in $s!$ with the ones left over from $p_i^{r_i-1}$ and obtain the desired result.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $m=\textup{rad}(n)$. Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ such that $a=dm+b$, where $d$ and $b$ are the unique quotient and remainder, respectively, of the Euclidean division. Then $a^{\varphi (n)}\equiv b^{\varphi (n)}\pmod{n}. $ In other words, powers of the form $u^{\varphi (n)}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are periodic with period $m,$ where furthermore $m^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ and we have that $m$ is the smallest non-trivial nilpotent of $n.$
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We have that $$a^{\varphi (n)}=(dm+b)^{\varphi (n)}=\sum_{k=0}^{\varphi (n)}{\binom{\varphi (n)}{k}(dm)^k b^{\varphi (n)-k}}. $$ We will show that $$\binom{\varphi (n)}{k}m^k\equiv 0 \pmod{n}$$ for all $k\geq 1.$ Then all terms of the binomial will vanish except for $k=0,$ which is precisely $b^{\varphi (n)}.$

By Lemma \ref{lem1} we know that $m^k\varphi (n)=n\varphi (m^k)$ and therefore $$\binom{\varphi (n)}{k}m^k=\binom{\varphi (n)}{k}n\cdot\frac{\varphi (m^k)}{\varphi (n)}.$$ If $n\mid m^k$ then $\varphi(n)\mid \varphi(m^k)$ and we have it. Otherwise, there exists at least one $p_i$ with $r_i>k.$ We know that $p_i^{r_i}=p_i^{k}\cdot p_i^{r_i-k}$ and $p_i^k\mid m^k. $ By Lemma \ref{lem2}, $p_i^{r_i-k}\mid \binom{\varphi (n)}{k}.$ Therefore, $\varphi (n)\mid \binom{\varphi (n)}{k}\cdot\varphi (m^k)$, and we have proven the claim.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
Let $S_m=\sum_{i=1}^m{i^{\varphi (m)}}\pmod{m}$, where $S_m<m$. Then $$\sum_{i=1}^n{i^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv\frac{n}{m}\cdot S_m\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
We know that $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has $\frac{n}{m}$ nilpotents, and each defines a sum-of-powers cycle of the form $i^{\varphi (n)}$, so it suffices to sum the first cycle and then multiply it by $\frac{n}{m}.$

We have that

$$S_m=\sum_{i=1}^m{i^{\varphi (m)}}\pmod{m}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^m{i^{\varphi (n)}}\pmod{m},$$

since $m\mid n$ and $i^{\varphi (m)}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_m.$ On the other hand, $S_m\equiv S_m+am$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n,$ with $a\geq 0$, and therefore $$\frac{n}{m}\cdot (S_m+am)\equiv\frac{n}{m}S_m+n\equiv\frac{n}{m}S_m\pmod{n},$$ and we can consider without loss of generality $a=0$ and $S_m<m.$

Then $$\frac{n} {m}S_m\equiv\frac{n}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m{i^{\varphi (m)}}\equiv\frac{n}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m{i^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^n{i^{\varphi (n)}}\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{inlc}
For all $n\in\mathbb{N},$ $$\sum_{i=1}^n{i^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi (d)\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}}\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $p_j$ be a prime divisor of $n$. If $n=p_j^{r_j}u,$ with $\gcd(p_j,u)=1,$ then $i^{\varphi (n)}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}$ if $p_j\mid i$ and $1$ otherwise, since in that case $\gcd(p_j,i)=1$ and $$\varphi (n)=\varphi (u)\cdot p_j^{r_j-1}(p_j-1)=\varphi (u)\cdot p_j^{r_j-1}\varphi (p_j),$$ and we can then apply Euler’s theorem. Let us verify that, for every prime divisor of $n$, the left and right sides of our hypothetical congruence coincide and, therefore, by the uniqueness of the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the congruence must necessarily hold.

The left side in $\mathbb{Z}_{p_j}$ is equivalent to

$$\#\left\{ i\in\mathbb{Z}_n / \gcd(p_j,i)=1\right\},$$

which is the same as

$$n-\frac{n}{p_j}\equiv -\frac{n}{p_j}\pmod{p_j}.$$

As for the right-hand side, $\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}$ is congruent in $\mathbb{Z}_{p_j}$ to $0$ if $p_j\mid\frac{n}{d}$ and to $1$ otherwise, so

$$\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi (d)\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv\sum_{p_j\nmid\frac{n}{d}}{\varphi (d)}\pmod{p_j}.$$

But this is the same as

$$\sum_{\substack{p_j^{r_j}\mid d\\d\mid n}}{\varphi (d)}=\sum_{a\mid \frac{n}{p_j^{r_j}}}{\varphi \left( ap_j^{r_j}\right)} =\sum_{a\mid \frac{n}{p_j^{r_j}}}{\varphi (a)\varphi \left( p_j^{r_j}\right)}=$$

$$=\varphi \left( p_j^{r_j}\right)\sum_{a\mid \frac{n}{p_j^{r_j}}}{\varphi (a)}=\varphi \left( p_j^{r_j}\right)\cdot\frac{n}{p_j^{r_j}}=\left ( p_j^{r_j}-p_j^{r_j-1}\right)\cdot\frac{n}{p_j^{r_j}}=n-\frac{n}{p_j},$$

which is congruent to $-\frac{n}{p_j}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{p_j}$, and we are done.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- obs-3: body_md -->
In the proof of Theorem \ref{inlc}, we also verified along the way—again using the Chinese Remainder Theorem—that the congruence in Theorem \ref{ilc2},

$$\sum_{i=1}^n{i^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv \sum_{p_i\mid n}{-\frac{n}{p_i}}\pmod{n},$$

holds for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, not just for $n$ free of squares. In fact, once again this statement is a special case of the Carlitz-von Staudt lemma mentioned in observation \ref{c-vs}. We remain within the conditions of the proposition since $\varphi(n)$ is even if $n\geq 3$ (although we have also verified this for $n=2$) and $p_i-1\mid\varphi(n)$ for every prime divisor $p_i\mid n$, and therefore it is not necessary to specify this in the summation index.
<!-- end obs-3 -->
<!-- cor-7: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be a composite number; then $n$ is a Giuga number if and only if

$$\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi (d)\cdot \left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\varphi (n)}}\equiv-1\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end cor-7 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
Given $n,k\in\mathbb{N}$, we define the arithmetic function $$G_k(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}{\varphi(n)\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^k}.$$
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
We say that a composite number $n\in\mathbb{N}$ is a Carmichael number if it satisfies the relation $b^n\equiv b\pmod{n}$ for all integers $b$.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- pro-1: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be a square-free number, and $p$ a prime divisor of $n$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\left(G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\right)^2+G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\equiv p^2+p\pmod{n}.$
    \item $p\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\equiv p^2\pmod{n}.$
    \item $G_{\varphi(n)}(2n)\equiv 2\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\pmod{n},$ regardless of the parity of $n$.
    \item If $n$ is a Giuga number, $G_{\varphi(n)}\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)$ is a solution to the equation $px^2-x-1\equiv 0 \pmod{n}.$
    \item If $n$ is a Carmichael number, $G_{n-1}(n)\equiv G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\pmod{n}.$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end pro-1 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We solve each of the above statements one by one:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\left(G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\right)^2\equiv\left( p^{\varphi(n)}+p-1\right)^2\equiv \left(p^{\varphi(n)}\right)^2+p^2+1+2p\cdot p^{\varphi(n)}-2p^ {\varphi(n)}-2p\equiv p^{\varphi(n)}+p^2+1+2p-2p^{\varphi(n)}-2p\equiv -p^{\varphi(n)}+p^2+1\equiv p^2+p-\left( p^{\varphi(n)} +p-1\right)\equiv p^2+p-G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\pmod{n},$ where we have used the fact that $p^{\varphi(n)}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ and acts as the identity element multiplied by $p$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
    \item $p^{\varphi(n)}\cdot \left(p^{\varphi(n)}+p-1\right)\equiv \left(p^{\varphi(n)}\right)^2+p\cdot p^{\varphi(n)}-p^ {\varphi(n)}\equiv p\pmod{n}$, and therefore $p\cdot p^{\varphi(n)}\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\equiv p\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\equiv p^2\pmod{n}.$
    \item We note that $G_{\varphi(n)}(2)=2^{\varphi(n)}+1$ and that $G_{\varphi(n)}(4)=2^{2\varphi(n)}+2^{\varphi(n)}+2.$ If we assume $n=2\cdot p_2\ldots p_s$,

    $$G_{\varphi(n)}(2n)\equiv G_{\varphi(n)}(4)\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(p_2\ldots p_s)\equiv$$ $$\equiv\left(2^{2\varphi(n)}+2^ {\varphi(n)}+2\right)\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(p_2\ldots p_s)\equiv$$ $$\equiv 2\left(2^{\varphi(n)}+1\right)\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(p_2\ldots p_s)\equiv 2\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\pmod{n}.$$

    For the odd case, it is trivial, since $n$ and $2$ have no common factors, that $G_{\varphi(n)}(2n)\equiv G_{\varphi(n)}(2)\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\equiv \left(2^{\varphi(n)}+1\right)\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\equiv 2 \cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\pmod{n}$ by Euler’s Theorem.

    \item We know that $$1\equiv\left( G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\right)^2\equiv\left( G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\right)^2\left( G_{\varphi(n)}\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)\right)^2\equiv$$ $$\equiv\left( p+(p-1)\cdot G_{\varphi(n)}(p)\right)\cdot\left( G_{\varphi(n)}\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)\right)^2\pmod{n},$$ using the previous properties 1 and 2 and the fact that $n$ is a Giuga number. We therefore have that $$1\equiv p\cdot \left( G_{\varphi(n)}(\frac{n}{p})\right)^2-\left( G_{\varphi(n)}(\frac{n}{p})\right)\pmod{n}, $$ and thus $\left( G_{\varphi(n)}(\frac{n}{p})\right)$ is a solution to the equation $px^2-x-1\equiv 0\pmod{n}.$
    \item This is an immediate result if we use Korselt’s criterion \cite{wright2015variants}, which states that a number $n$ is a Carmichael number if and only if it is square-free and for every prime divisor of $n$, $(p-1)\mid (n-1).$ Knowing this,

$$G_{n-1}(n)\equiv \prod_{j=1}^s\left(p_j^{n-1}+p_j-1\right)\equiv -1\cdot \prod_{j=2}^s{\left(\left(p_j^{p_1-1}\right)^k+p_j-1\right)}\equiv$$ $$\equiv -1\cdot \prod_{j=2}^s{(1+p_j-1)}\equiv -\frac{n}{p_1}\pmod{p_1}.$$ Since we can do this for every $p_i\mid n,$ by Theorem \ref{ilc2} we have arrived at

$$G_{n-1}(n)\equiv -\sum_{p\mid n}{\frac{n}{p}}\equiv G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\pmod{n}.$$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- cor-8: body_md -->
The final result implies that if a number is both a Carmichael and a Giuga number, then it is a counterexample to the Agoh–Giuga Conjecture, a classic result in the study of this conjecture that has been obtained here via an alternative route. The converse of this result is not true even among square-free numbers. The first square-free number satisfying $G_{n-1}(n)\equiv G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\pmod{n}$ is 65, and it is not a Carmichael number. We will explore this issue further in the next section.
<!-- end cor-8 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$. We say that an idempotent $e\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ is prime if it is of the form $e\equiv p^{\varphi(n)}\pmod{n}$, where $p$ is a prime number and a divisor of $n$.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{idp}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $e$ be an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Then $e\equiv d^{\varphi(n)}\pmod{n}$, where $d=\gcd(n,e)$. Furthermore, $d$ is unitary.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We know that $e\equiv a^{\varphi(n)}\pmod{n}$ for a unitary divisor $a$ of $n$. Let us show that precisely $\gcd(n,e)=a$. First, $e-a^{\varphi(n)}=kn$, so $e=a^{\varphi(n)}+kn$ with $a\mid n$. Therefore, $a\mid e$ and $a\mid d=\gcd(n,e)$.

We can thus write $d=af,$ with $f\in\mathbb{N},$ $\gcd\left(f,\frac{n}{a}\right)=1.$ On the one hand,

$$d^{\varphi(n)}\equiv a^{\varphi(n)}f^{\varphi(n)}\equiv a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv e\pmod{\frac{n}{a}}$$

and furthermore $d^{\varphi(n)}\equiv 0\pmod{a}.$ On the other hand, $a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv e\pmod{\frac{n}{a}}$ and $a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv 0\pmod{a}. $ Therefore, by the uniqueness of the Chinese Remainder Theorem, since $\gcd\left(a,\frac{n}{a}\right)=1,$ we obtain

$$a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv d^{\varphi(n)}\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$; $n$ is a Giuga number if and only if the prime idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are the set 

$$I_p=\left\{1-\frac{n}{p}, p\text{ prime, }p\mid n\right\}$$
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We start with the implication from left to right. We know \cite{borwein1996giuga} that a number is a Giuga number if and only if $p\mid\left(\frac{n}{p}-1\right)$ for every prime divisor $p$ of $n$. Following a line of reasoning used in the recent article \cite{mondal2024idempotents}, where they classify all idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}_n$, since $\gcd\left(p,\frac{n}{p}\right)=1$ when $n$ is square-free (i.e., $p$ is a unit divisor), we have that

$$\frac{n}{p}\cdot p=n\mid \left[\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)^2-\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)\right]$$

and, therefore, $\frac{n}{p}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$. We know that $e=1-\frac{n}{p}$ is also an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$, and in fact is the prime idempotent associated with the divisor $p$. To see this, it suffices to check that $p\mid e$, which is true since, as $n$ is a Giuga number, $p\mid\left(\frac{n}{p}-1\right)$ and, furthermore, given that $q\not=p$ is a prime divisor of $n$, since $q\mid -\frac{n}{p}$, then $q\nmid e$ and, therefore, $gcd(n,e)=p$, which proves that $1-\frac{n}{p}$ is the prime idempotent associated with $p$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$.

For the converse implication, we know that $1-\frac{n}{p}$ is a prime idempotent and, in particular, $\frac{n}{p}$ is also an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Then

$$\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)^2\equiv\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)\pmod{n}.$$ 

This implies that

$$\frac{n^2}{p^2}-\frac{n}{p}=kn$$

for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, and thus $n-p=kp^2$, which automatically implies that $p^2\mid (n-p)$, and this is equivalent to $p\mid\left(\frac{n}{p}-1\right).$ Therefore, $n$ is a Giuga number.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- cor-9: body_md -->
\label{giugacor}
$n\in\mathbb{N}$ is a Giuga number if and only if $\frac{n}{p}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ for every prime divisor $p$ of $n$.
<!-- end cor-9 -->
<!-- cor-10: body_md -->
If $n$ is a Giuga number, then $$G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\equiv\prod_{i=1}^s\left(\frac{p_i^2-n}{p_i}\right)\equiv -1\pmod{n},$$ but it is trivial to verify that the converse implication is not true.
<!-- end cor-10 -->
<!-- pro-2: body_md -->
\label{carm}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be a Carmichael number. The prime idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are the numbers of the form $p^{n-1}$, where $p$ is a prime divisor of $n$.
<!-- end pro-2 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
$\left(p^{n-1}\right)^2\equiv p^{2n-2}\equiv p^n\cdot p^{n-2}\equiv p\cdot p^{n-2}\equiv p^{n-1}\pmod{n},$ where we have used the fact that for a Carmichael number, we always have $b^n\equiv b\pmod{n}. $ On the other hand, it follows immediately from the definition and the fact that a Carmichael number is square-free that these idempotents are prime.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- cor-11: body_md -->
The converse is not true, not even among square-free numbers. $65$ is the smallest square-free number satisfying $65=5\cdot 13$, and its prime idempotents are $5^{64}\equiv 40\pmod{65}$ and $13^{64}\equiv 26\pmod{65}.$
<!-- end cor-11 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be a composite number; we say that $n$ is a Semi-Carmichael number (hereinafter referred to as SC number) if, for every divisor $d$ of $n$, we have $d^n\equiv d\pmod{n}.$
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- pro-3: body_md -->
\label{semi}
Let $n$ be a SC number.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $n$ is square-free.
        \item Its prime idempotents are the numbers of the form $p^{n-1}$, where $p$ is a prime divisor of $n$, and the converse is also true if we require that $n$ be composite.
        \item $G_{n-1}(n)\equiv G_{\varphi (n)}(n)\pmod{n}$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end pro-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
To prove that $n$ is square-free, suppose that $n=p^rm$ with $r>1$ and $\gcd(m,p)=1$. By the SC number definition, $p^n \equiv p \pmod{n}$ and, since $r>1$, $p^n \equiv p \pmod{p^2}$. Since $n$ is composite and therefore greater than or equal to $2$, we must have $p \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$, which is impossible. Therefore, $r = 1$ for every prime divisor $p$ of $n$.

For the second part, given a SC number $n$, we have, as we already showed, that

$$\left( p^{n-1}\right)^2\equiv p^{2n-2}\equiv p^n\cdot p^{n-2}\equiv p^{n-1}\pmod{n}$$

and, since $n$ is square-free, $\gcd(n,p^{n-1})=p$ and therefore $p^{n-1}$ is a prime idempotent.

For the converse, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that its prime idempotents are of the form $p^{n-1}$, where $p$ is a prime divisor of $n$. Then

$$\left(p^{n-1}\right)^2\equiv p^{2n-2}\equiv p^{n-1}\pmod{n},$$

and this implies that

$$p^n\cdot p^{n-1}\equiv p^n\pmod{n}.$$

If we consider a divisor $q$ of $n$ coprime with $p$, then $p^{n-1}$ has an inverse in $Z_q$ and we can state that

$$p^{n-1}\equiv 1\pmod{q}\implies p^n\equiv p\pmod{q},$$

and since it is trivial that $p^n\equiv p\pmod{p}$, using the Chinese Remainder Theorem we have that $p^n\equiv p\pmod{n}$ for every prime divisor $p$ of $n$ and, therefore, since $n$ is composite, it is also an SC number.

For the last statement, it suffices to use the previous section and Lemma \ref{idp} to show that

$$G_{n-1}(n)\equiv \prod_{e\in I_p(n)}{e+\gcd(e,n)-1}\equiv G_{\varphi(n)}(n)\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- cor-12: body_md -->
\label{corguigacarmichael}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be a composite number; $n$ is a Giuga and SC number if and only if for every prime divisor $p$ of $n$, 
    
$$p^{n-1}\equiv1-\frac{n}{p}\pmod{n}.$$
<!-- end cor-12 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The implication from left to right follows immediately from what we have seen so far, since for every prime divisor $p$ of $n$, its associated prime idempotent is, on the one hand, $1-\frac{n}{p}$ because it is a Giuga number divisor, and also $p^{n-1}$ because it is a SC number divisor; therefore, both values are equal modulo $n$.

Regarding the converse implication, given $p$ a prime divisor of $n$,
    
$$\left(p^{n-1}\right)\left(1-\frac{n}{p}\right)\equiv p^{n-1}-np^{n-2}\equiv p^{n-1}\pmod{n},$$

where $n-2\geq1$ since $n$ is composite, so $1-\frac{n}{p}$ is an idempotent for every prime divisor $p$ of $n$. By Corollary \ref{giugacor}, $n$ is a Giuga number and, in particular, is square-free. On the other hand,

$$p\cdot p^{n-1}\equiv p^n\equiv p-n\equiv p\pmod{n},$$

and since $n$ is composite and this holds for every prime divisor of $n$, then $n$ is a SC number, although this is also immediate since we have shown in \ref{semi} that every composite number whose prime idempotents are of the form $p^{n-1}$ is a SC number, and these idempotents are prime since $n$ is Giuga and consequently square-free, and $\gcd(n,p^{n-1})=p$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
